clue.text: Noted automatic repeater

parts.note: a clockwork device that plays musical notes over and over by itself; 'Noted' means furnished with notes, not famous

explanation.surface: A well-known machine that keeps repeating itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' reads as 'famous' but means 'playing notes'; the repeater is a mechanism that plays the same tune when wound.
explanation.definitionFit: A wind-up toy with a cylinder of pins plays a tune mechanically and repeats it.

clue.text: Catty remark !

parts.note: catty usually means spiteful, but here it is a remark made by a cat

explanation.surface: A spiteful comment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catty' looks like 'spiteful'; the remark is literally a cat's, the cry a cat makes.
explanation.definitionFit: The sound a cat utters, spelt in British fashion, is the only remark a cat makes.

clue.text: Literary watchman

explanation.surface: A bookish lookout.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spectator is a long-running British weekly magazine of politics and literature; a spectator is also someone who watches.
explanation.definitionFit: The London weekly review of books and politics bears the name, and an onlooker is one who watches.

clue.text: Unusual charge latent in a housewarming

indicators.note: unusual tells the solver that the following letters are arranged in an unusual way

explanation.surface: An odd fee hiding in a party for a new home.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR dropped the 'a' before 'housewarming'. 'housewarming' looks like a party but is literal: a system that warms a house. The fodder is CHARGE LATENT IN, fourteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A boiler and radiators heating every room from one source is literally a means of warming a house.

clue.text: Roped and led Neddy round inside

indicators.note: inside places the donkey and the ring within the word led

parts.note: taken as written
Neddy is a familiar British name for a donkey, an ass
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: A cowboy roped a donkey and led it round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neddy' is a British pet name for a donkey. 'and' is a link, and 'Roped' at the front is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Caught with a noosed rope thrown from horseback, as cowboys catch cattle.

clue.text: One of the townsfolk sportingly goes to the wall

definitions.text: One of the townsfolk sportingly goes to the wall

parts.words: One of the townsfolk sportingly goes to the wall
parts.note: at Eton the boys boarding in town houses play the scholars in the Wall Game, so one of them literally goes to the wall

explanation.surface: A townsman who fails, as a business going to the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes to the wall' means fails, but here it is literal. At Eton College the pupils who are not scholars are called by a Latin word for townspeople, and they play the scholars in the annual Wall Game against a brick wall.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin-derived name for a townsman is used at Eton for boys who board in houses rather than in College.

clue.text: Sword-carrying Frenchman

explanation.surface: A French swordsman.
explanation.walkthrough: A frog is the loop on a belt that holds a sword or bayonet scabbard; 'Frog' is also old British slang for a French person.
explanation.definitionFit: A belt attachment holding a scabbard carries a sword, and the slang nickname for a native of France matches the second sense.

clue.text: Mounted gunners hold a return party for her

indicators.note: hold means the gunners' abbreviation contains the other piece

parts.note: RHA is the Royal Horse Artillery, gunners on horseback

indicators.note: return means the words a and party are read backwards

parts.note: a do is a party

explanation.surface: Cavalry gunners throw a return party for a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns only 'a party', not the gunners; 'her' alone is the definition, any woman's name fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhoda is a woman's first name, so it stands for any 'her'.

clue.text: It makes capital cover in the Highlands

definitions.text: It makes capital cover in the Highlands

parts.words: It makes capital cover in the Highlands
parts.note: a Scottish woollen cap; 'capital cover' is a hat for the head, not a fine shelter

explanation.surface: Something that provides excellent shelter in the Scottish mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital cover' reads as 'excellent shelter', but 'capital' is used for 'of the head': a head covering, the boat-shaped Scottish cap.
explanation.definitionFit: The creased woollen cap with ribbons at the back is traditional Highland headgear.

clue.text: Risk wrong ropes in order to get the job going forward

indicators.note: in order says the jumbled letters must be put into their proper order

explanation.surface: Taking a chance with the wrong ropes to get a job done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' looks like the anagram signal but is fodder: all fourteen letters of RISK WRONG ROPES are put 'in order'.
explanation.definitionFit: A task still under way and not yet finished is described as continuing, advancing towards completion.

clue.text: Hell Lake

explanation.surface: A fiery underworld lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR read 'Hall' for the printed 'Hell'. Avernus is a crater lake near Naples which the Romans thought was the entrance to the underworld, so its name also stood for the underworld itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman poets used the name of the volcanic lake near Cumae for the underworld, the abode of the dead, as well as for the lake.

clue.text: "Can honour's voice the silent dust.?" (Gray)

definitions.text: Can honour's voice the silent dust

parts.words: Can honour's voice the silent dust
parts.note: a line of Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard with its verb missing; the solver supplies the verb meaning to stir up or rouse

explanation.surface: A quotation from Thomas Gray with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash for the missing word. Gray's Elegy asks whether honour's voice can rouse the dead in their graves; the gap takes a seven-letter verb meaning to stir or call forth.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb in Gray's line means to rouse or stir into action, which is what honour's voice cannot do to the dead.

clue.text: Does its reservoir supply only 500 Irishmen ?

definitions.text: Does its reservoir supply only 500 Irishmen ?

parts.words: Does its reservoir supply only 500 Irishmen
parts.note: an Irish city and county whose name splits as a liquid supply set aside for the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: A question about a town's reservoir serving only five hundred people.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the place name as three words: a reservoir's water 'for D', D being the Roman numeral 500. Waterford is a city in the south-east of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish city on the River Suir, known for its crystal glassware, is the place whose name the question splits.

clue.text: A metal strike, we hear, in Selangor

indicators.note: signals that the word for a ringing blow on metal is spoken, and a different spelling sounds the same

parts.note: a clang is the ringing sound of metal being struck

explanation.surface: Somebody hears a metallic bang somewhere in Malaysia.
explanation.walkthrough: Selangor is a state of Malaysia; Klang is a town there, which sounds the same as CLANG.
explanation.definitionFit: Klang is a royal town and port district within the Malaysian state on the Strait of Malacca.

clue.text: To be means not to be without this organ

definitions.text: To be means not to be without this organ

parts.words: To be means not to be without this organ
parts.note: an organ one cannot live without; 'to be' (to live) depends on having it, and the word also means essential

explanation.surface: A philosophical riddle about existence and an organ of the body.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue echoes Hamlet's 'To be or not to be'. A heart or brain is a vital organ: without it you cannot be, i.e. live; the adjective also means indispensable.
explanation.definitionFit: Organs such as the heart are called essential to life, from the Latin for life, so being alive requires them.

clue.text: Parson has debts incurred for others

parts.note: a vicar is a parish priest, a parson
IOUs are written promises to pay debts

explanation.surface: A clergyman runs up debts on behalf of other people.
explanation.walkthrough: IOUs ('I owe you') are notes acknowledging debts.
explanation.definitionFit: Something experienced or suffered in place of another person is done by proxy, on their behalf.

clue.text: Where on some railway journeys there may be many a slip…

definitions.text: Where on some railway journeys there may be many a slip…

parts.words: Where on some railway journeys there may be many a slip
parts.note: the proverb 'there's many a slip twixt cup and lip' points to drinks spilt in a moving train's restaurant carriage

explanation.surface: A warning about accidents on train journeys.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing dots finish the proverb 'many a slip twixt cup and lip': on a swaying train it is in the restaurant carriage that soup and tea get spilt on the way to the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway carriage serving meals is where diners raise cups and spoons to their lips while the train rocks.

clue.text: It seems this seat of learning has a way to cross the river dry-shod

definitions.text: It seems this seat of learning has a way to cross the river dry-shod

parts.words: It seems this seat of learning has a way to cross the river dry-shod
parts.note: the university city's name splits into its river and a structure for crossing it without wading

explanation.surface: A university town provides a dry crossing over its river.
explanation.walkthrough: The city's name reads as its river, the Cam, plus a bridge, a way across without getting wet feet.
explanation.definitionFit: The English university city on the River Cam is the seat of learning described.

clue.text: Chalcedony extracted from inner coal

indicators.note: the letters are pulled out of the words that follow and set in a new order

explanation.surface: A gemstone dug out from a coal seam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extracted from' suggests a hidden word, but no run of 'inner coal' gives the answer: its nine letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornelian (carnelian) is a reddish variety of the mineral chalcedony used in seals and jewellery.

clue.text: Artistic style of Mac the Knife ?

definitions.text: Artistic style of Mac the Knife ?

parts.words: Artistic style of Mac the Knife
parts.note: a painter laying on thick paint with a palette knife, so a painter armed with a knife works this way

explanation.surface: A question about the art of the gangster in The Threepenny Opera song.
explanation.walkthrough: Mac the Knife is the murderous gangster in Brecht and Weill's song; a painter who uses a palette knife lays the paint on thickly, the technique named here.
explanation.definitionFit: The painting technique applies paint in thick ridges, often with a palette knife.

clue.text: Far from bold, this system

explanation.surface: Someone timid about a system.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition stands for the body's network of nerves, the nervous system.
explanation.definitionFit: Timid and anxious people are far from bold, and the body's network of nerves and brain is called by the same adjective.

clue.text: Strange, my joining this game :

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: Someone joins a game and finds it odd.
explanation.walkthrough: RUM is British informal for odd; MY is taken as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Rummy is a card game in which players collect sets and runs.

clue.text: How audiences feel about part of the play ?

parts.note: re is a short word meaning concerning or about
an act is one of the main divisions of a play

explanation.surface: A question about how theatregoers feel about a scene.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads as a description: what audiences do in response to a performance is to respond, so the verb fills 'audiences ___'.
explanation.definitionFit: Audiences respond to what they see, showing a feeling in answer to the performance.

clue.text: Decapitation — legal yet terrible

indicators.note: removing the head of the word means losing its first letter

parts.note: lawful means permitted by law, legal

explanation.surface: Execution by beheading is lawful but horrible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decapitation' reads as part of the picture of an execution; it tells you to drop the first letter of LAWFUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Awful and terrible are synonyms for something very bad or dreadful.

clue.text: Cigar rolled with rope is soothing

indicators.note: rolled suggests the letters are turned over and over into a new order, as a cigar is rolled

explanation.surface: Smoking a cigar rolled up with rope proves calming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rolled' looks like a description of the cigar but asks for the letters of CIGAR and ROPE to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Paregoric is an old camphorated opium tincture, and as an adjective means pain-relieving or calming.

clue.text: Trouble up here — the Frenchman's was novel

explanation.surface: Trouble ahead in a French novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up the creek' means in trouble; 'Frenchman's Creek' is Daphne du Maurier's 1941 novel of a Cornish lady and a French pirate.
explanation.definitionFit: A small tidal inlet is where one is stuck when in difficulty, and it completes the title of du Maurier's romance.

clue.text: Right side finishes but does wrong

parts.note: in cricket the off side is the right-hand side of the field for a right-handed batsman
ends means finishes, as a verb or plural noun

explanation.surface: A team's right flank finishes off its play but commits a foul.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the off side is the half of the field to a right-handed batsman's right as he faces the bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: To offend is to commit a wrong or transgress, as an offender breaks the law.

clue.text: Like Mariana's visitor, or Bill as a cause of action?

definitions.text: Like Mariana's visitor, or Bill as a cause of action?

parts.words: Like Mariana's visitor, or Bill as a cause of action
parts.note: Tennyson's Mariana waits for a lover who never comes, and an unpaid bill past its date can be sued on

explanation.surface: A comparison between a jilted woman's absent caller and an unpaid account.
explanation.walkthrough: In Tennyson's poem 'Mariana' she repeats 'He cometh not', so her visitor is late; a bill unpaid past its date likewise gives grounds to sue.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the awaited lover and the unpaid account are late, past the expected time.

clue.text: Taken for a court gown

parts.note: a barrister who becomes a Queen's Counsel is said to take the fabric of the gown worn by senior counsel

explanation.surface: A gown mistaken for one worn at court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken for' reads as 'mistaken for', but in Britain a barrister appointed King's or Queen's Counsel 'takes silk', after the silk gown that rank wears in court.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine fabric of a senior barrister's gown names the rank itself, so promotion to senior counsel is described with it.

clue.text: Drink to Steed's impertinence!

parts.note: a steed is a horse, so steed's is horse's
neck is British slang for cheek or nerve

explanation.surface: A toast to the cheek of someone called Steed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neck' is British informal for cheek or brazen nerve. A horse's neck is a cocktail of brandy or bourbon with ginger ale and a long spiral of lemon peel.
explanation.definitionFit: The cocktail of spirit and ginger ale is named for its curling lemon peel garnish.
